title: ‘Satyagraha’ website launched by Rahul Gandhi: What is it?
author: The Hindu Bureau
content_html:
Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi on Saturday (October 3, 2026) launched the ‘Satyagraha’ digital platform to map resistance movements across the country.

This comes as Opposition leaders, civil society and youth-led organisations continue their protests in various parts of the country to demand the removal of the Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, over alleged disparities in handling the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.

देशभर में लोग अपने हक़ के लिए लड़ रहे हैं - और अक्सर अकेले लड़ रहे हैं। Gen Z, छात्र, किसान, आदिवासी, दलित, महिलाएँ - हर संघर्ष की अपनी कहानी है। पर जो आवाज़ अकेली उठती है, वो अक्सर दब जाती है। 'सत्याग्रह' इन्हीं आवाज़ों को एक नक्शे पर साथ लाने की पहल है। बापू ने यही सिखाया था - सच सबसे बड़ा हथियार है। पर उससे भी बड़ा हथियार है, एकता में सच के साथ खड़े होना। अगर आप भी किसी अन्याय से लड़ रहे हैं - अपनी कहानी भेजिए। दो मिनट लगेंगे। आपकी कहानी नक्शे पर आएगी। आप देखेंगे कि आपकी तरह और कौन-कौन लड़ रहा है। और मैं जो कर सकता हूँ, करूँगा - संसद में, सड़क पर, खत लिखकर, जहां भी मेरी ज़रूरत हो वहां आपके साथ खड़े होकर - नेता विपक्ष के रूप में ये मेरी ज़िम्मेदारी है। अपने सत्याग्रह को कहानी मुझे यहां बताएं 👉 https://t.co/hJ8iARr5La

— Rahul Gandhi (@RahulGandhi) October 3, 2026

What is the ‘Satyagraha website?’

In a post on X announcing the initiative, Mr. Gandhi said that people across the country were fighting for their rights and were “too often fighting alone”. He then listed Gen Z, students, farmers, Adivasis, Dalits, and women among those involved in different struggles.

“‘Satyagraha’ is an initiative to bring these voices together on one map, the Congress leader added.

In a video posted on his social media handle, Mr. Gandhi said that the “truth was being suppressed” and that, as the Leader of the Opposition, it is his responsibility to help in the resistance against this. Later,he said the ‘Satyagraha’ platform had received over 10,000 responses in nine hours after it went live. “That’s how many struggles Indians are already fighting — quietly, convinced no one was listening. We are listening. Every submission will be read,” he added.

Satyagraha went live 9 hours ago. Since then, more than 10,000 people and groups have come forward. That's how many struggles Indians are already fighting - quietly, convinced no one was listening. We are listening. Every submission will be read. Already, we see stories in the topics of education, corruption, social justice, farmers, labour, health, women's safety, land and environment. Our team will go through each one, work out how we can help, and reach out where more details are needed. Where any genuine struggle needs to be amplified to be resolved, we will do it. This is only the beginning. Satyagraha isn't a one-day campaign. It will run for years, and it will stand with every andolan, big or small. Thank you for speaking up and for standing up for the Constitution. If you haven't yet, tell me your story 👉 https://t.co/hJ8iARr5La

— Rahul Gandhi (@RahulGandhi) October 3, 2026

How does the website work?

The “Satyagraha” website works as a catalogue based on input from its users. There is a form through which an individual or group can list their issues, based on a number of categories. 

Here are the steps to follow:

1. Log on to the Satyagraha website.

2. Click on the ‘raise your voice’ button.

3. Navigate to the form and choose if you want to file your issue as an individual or a group.

4. Fill details like your name, State/Union Territory, district, and contact number.

5. Choose the category of your cause from the drop-down menu.

6. Elaborate on your issue in the ‘what do you want people to know’ box.

7. Share a photo or video of your cause (optional).

8. Fill out a captcha for verification and click on ‘raise your voice’ button.

What are the categories that the issues can be listed in? 

The issues can categorized under the following categories on the Satyagraha website: 

  • Land rights.
  • Healthcare access
  • Caste-based discrimination
  • Labour rights
  • Environmental justice
  • Women’s safety
  • Farmer issues
  • Education access
  • Other 

What steps are taken after a citizen files the issue? 

The website lists three steps that happen after filing the issue.

It says that every issue is read and reviewed by the team. It is then pinned on a map of India in the state of the grievance. The map is available for viewing on the website.

The final step is that selected issues from the repository may be “raised through social media, press conferences, Parliament etc.”

title: El Niño draws ‘Kasai Pitta' out in Rayalaseema scrub lands
author: K. Umashanker
content_html:
In the arid scrub of Rayalaseema, where summer lasts nearly half the year, a small masked predator has returned to its perch. The butcher bird, locally called the ‘kasai pitta’, is being sighted again across the region’s driest patches.

The long-tailed shrike, Lanius schach, is seen in stony wastelands and thorn scrub around Galiveedu, Tamballapalle, Rayachoti and Lakkireddipalle in Annamayya; Vempalle, Jammalamadugu and Pulivendula in Kadapa; Gooty, Tadipatri, Penukonda and Kadiri in combined Anantapur; Adoni and Pattikonda in Kurnool; and Nagari, Puthalapattu and Punganur in Chittoor. It is also sighted along the Penna River belt and fringes of the Erramala and Palakonda ranges in Nandyal and Kadapa.

Perched silently on a tree trunk or power line across fields and forest buffers, the bird with a black bandit mask scans the parched ground. It swoops like a dart at lizards, grasshoppers, mice, and small snakes. Farmers often find its prey pinned on thorns or barbed wire, its open-air meat shop.

It is widely called kasai pitta. It impales prey and displays it like a butcher shop. It is incredibly clever and very cruel to its prey, says Krishnappa Kumar, 24, a horticulture farmer from Mandipeta Kotur in Palamaner mandal.

Groundnut farmer Ramireddy Kasireddy of Galiveedu in Annamayya says the bird, though small, does not spare even snakes of moderate size. “If a snake is small, the bird handles it easily. If it’s a young snake or moderate lizard, it lifts them by the tail or spine and drops them on thorny bushes, thus arresting prey, and impales them live before eating at leisure.,” he said.

Dr V. V. Balasubramanyam, associate professor of Zoology at Sri Krishnadevaraya University, Anantapur, says, “Impaling compensates for weak talons. With poor grip, it uses thorns as forks to tear flesh and store food for lean days.”

The bird is listed as Least Concern by IUCN, with a stable global population, and is not endangered globally. But in Rayalaseema, particularly in the south, it faces severe local stress. Scrublands are vanishing for housing layouts, and intensive pesticide use in mango, tomato, and groundnut belts in Chittoor, Annamayya, and Anantapur kills its insect prey. This El Niño year, the breeding of grasshoppers and beetles that feed its chicks fell drastically.

A senior forest official in Sri Sathya Sai district said that in an El Niño year, sightings became more frequent. With green cover thinned, spotting prey on barren ground is easier, so birds are visible more often. But vast fields are left uncultivated, and grasslands wither, so actually finding prey is harder. Their breeding and survival are in question if the scrub ecosystem collapses.

title: Tamil Nadu byelections: why are only two constituencies going to polls instead of seven?
author: The Hindu Bureau
content_html:
The Election Commission of India (ECI) had notified byelections to only two constituencies – Dharapuram and Madurantakam – in Tamil Nadu, even as five other constituencies remain vacant.

Resignation of six AIADMK MLAs

C. Vijayabaskar (Viralimalai), M.R. Vijayabhaskar (Karur), Esakki Subaya (Ambasamudram), P. Sathyabama (Dharapuram), K. Maragatham Kumaravel (Madurantakam) and S. Jayakumar (Perundurai) had won the Assembly elections this year as AIADMK candidates. They, however, resigned as MLAs shortly thereafter, before joining the ruling TVK. Apart from these constituencies, Tiruchirappalli (East) was vacated by TVK chief and Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay, who had won from Perambur Assembly seat as well.

Byelections are being held only in Madurantakam and Dharapuram, where K. Maragatham Kumaravel and P. Sathyabama, respectively, had been elected as AIADMK MLAs before resigning from the party and subsequently joining the TVK. The ruling party has fielded them as its candidates for the bypolls from the respective constituencies.

Madurantakam in northern Tamil Nadu and Dharapuram in the western region will go to the polls on October 6 to elect their representatives to the Assembly.

In all, seven constituencies are without MLAs. Byelections are required to be held within six months of a seat falling vacant, except under exceptional circumstances.

The legal bar on conducting a byelection to the Perundurai Assembly constituency had ended following the rejection of an election petition concerning the constituency on September 8, 2026, the EC submitted before the Madras High Court.

As far as the other four constituencies – Tiruchi East, Ambasamudram, Viralimalai and Karur – were concerned, the EC said byelections could not be notified until the election petitions, which included pleas to declare either the petitioners or other candidates as returned candidates, were decided.

Tiruchi East bypoll

Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay, who vacated Tiruchi East and retained Perambur after winning from both seats in the Assembly elections, had contended that he resigned even before an election petition was filed by DMK candidate S. Inigo Irudayaraj. The EC, however, said the timing of the resignation was immaterial.

The Commission said it would make no difference whether an election petition was filed before or after the resignation, as the constituency could face an anomalous situation, in which it was represented by two individuals if another candidate was subsequently declared the returned candidate by the election tribunal, the High Court, after a byelection had been held.

ECI, government differ over bypolls

The non-conduct of byelections to five Assembly constituencies in Tamil Nadu for an indefinite period would deprive several lakh people in those constituencies of democratically elected MLAs to represent their interests, causes, and grievances, the Chief Minister told the Madras High Court.

He made the submission in a counter-affidavit to a public interest litigation that had sought an interim stay, on July 10, 2026, on the conduct of byelections to Tiruchi East, Perundurai, Ambasamudram, Viralimalai, and Karur.

Claiming that the deferment of the byelections was “neither indefinite nor indiscriminate”, the EC said the bar would come to an end immediately after the election tribunal disposed of a plea, made along with an election petition, seeking to declare either the petitioner or another candidate as the returned candidate.

“This has already happened for the Perundurai constituency,” the Commission said. It also pointed out that Section 86(7) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, requires every election petition to be disposed of as expeditiously as possible, with an endeavour to conclude the trial within six months.

title: Thiruvananthapuram Corporation: R. Sreelekha’s resignation bid puts BJP in a spot
author: The Hindu Bureau
content_html:
For the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), former IPS officer R. Sreelekha’s move to quit as ward councillor in the Thiruvananthapuram Corporation, poses the threat of weakening its grip on the high-profile civic body.

If she formally tenders her resignation to the Corporation secretary, it would reduce the party’s tally in the 101-ward Municipal Corporation from 50 to 49, as well as necessitating a bypoll in the Sasthamangalam ward.

Of the two independents in the council, the BJP has the support of Pattoor Radhakrishnan, who heads the town planning standing committee. The other independent councillor, Sudheesh Kumar of the Poundkadavu ward, while not openly aligned with the BJP, had supported it in the contentious issue of extending leave to BJP councillor R. Sugathan. Mr. Sugathan was arrested under the Kerala Anti-Social Activities (Prevention) Act and is currently lodged in prison.

On the other hand, the BJP does not face an imminent threat of losing the Corporation as it still has more seats than the UDF and LDF and given the slim chance of the opposing fronts joining forces to topple it, say experts.

In the 2025 local body polls in Keralam, the BJP had wrested Thiruvananthapuram Corporation from the CPI(M)-led LDF, creating national-level headlines. It had emerged as the single largest party with 50 seats. The CPI(M)-led LDF was pushed down to 29 seats while the Congress-led UDF had won 19.

The January 12, 2026, special election to the Vizhinjam ward (election in 2025 had been put off due to the death of a candidate) saw the UDF wresting the ward and increasing its tally to 20.

According to Mayor V.V. Rajesh, Ms. Sreelekha had cited personal inconveniences as the reason and that the BJP was trying to “resolve issues.”

On their part, the LDF and the UDF are keenly watching the developments. Speaking to reporters on Saturday, LDF convener T.P. Ramakrishnan said the Thiruvananthapuram district committees of the CPI(M) and the LDF will take a clear stand by studying the developments. The BJP cannot continue in power and Ms. Sreelekha’s decision reflects the degree of unrest in the BJP camp, he said.

Speaking to The Hindu, Congress leader and UDF Parliamentary Party leader in the council K.S. Sabarinadhan indicated that his party was closely watching the developments. “Let it first be confirmed that she has resigned. But she has not been active in the ward during the last six months. If a bypoll takes place, we do believe that we can win,” Mr. Sabarinadhan said.

In the 2025 local body polls in Keralam, the BJP had wrested Thiruvananthapuram Corporation from the CPI(M)-led LDF, creating national-level headlines. It had emerged as the single largest party with 50 seats. The CPI(M)-led LDF was pushed down to 29 seats while the Congress-led UDF had won 19.
The January 12, 2026, special election to the Vizhinjam ward (election in 2025 had been put off due to the death of a candidate) saw the UDF wresting the ward and increasing its tally to 20.
According to Mayor V.V. Rajesh, Ms. Sreelekha had cited personal inconveniences as the reason and that the BJP was trying to “resolve issues.”
On their part, the LDF and the UDF are keenly watching the developments.  Speaking to reporters on Saturday, LDF convener T.P. Ramakrishnan said the Thiruvananthapuram district committees of the CPI(M) and the LDF will take a clear stand by studying the developments. The BJP cannot continue in power and Ms. Sreelekha’s decision reflects the degree of unrest in the BJP camp, he said.
Speaking to
The Hindu
, Congress leader and UDF Parliamentary Party leader in the council K.S. Sabarinadhan  indicated that his party was closely watching the developments. “Let it first be confirmed that she has resigned. But she has not been active in the ward during the last six months. If a bypoll takes place, we do believe that we can win,” Mr. Sabarinadhan said.

title: Kerala State Drugs Control dept. seeks curbs on inter-State drug procurement to ensure traceability
author: Aathira Haridas
content_html:
In a bid to ensure traceability of drugs, the Kerala State Drugs Control department has sent a letter to the Keralam government seeking an interim restriction on pharmaceutical firms directly procuring medicines from other States.

The department has sought the restriction for a period of six months, during which the firms would be required to procure medicines through authorised medical depots within Keralam.

Why the restriction?

“One of the challenges we face is ensuring the traceability of medicines being sold within the State,” said an official with the department. “A trend we have been observing is that medicines brought in for institutional supply are being sold in the general market. While these medicines may themselves be genuine and original products, their outer packaging gets altered. Medicines for institutional supply are available at heavily subsidised rates, and these are pushed into the market again, where they are sold at regular market prices. This kind of diversion is happening in other States, which is why the request was made,” he added.

According to the official, it was after the implementation of the Goods and Services Tax (GST) that retailers were permitted to procure medicines from other States, making it difficult to trace the sources of medicines and their manufacturers.

“At present, anyone can purchase medicines from anywhere, making it difficult to trace them. We will not be able to cross-check with suppliers in other States, and quite often they will not respond to our communications. But if the medicines are purchased from within the State, the authorised depot is directly connected with the company; there are no middlemen involved, and it will be easy for us to verify,” the official said.

‘Legal issues’

He, however, noted that it could be difficult to implement this as direct procurement has been allowed since the implementation of GST, and there could be some legal issues. “Our intention is to implement this for a short time and then observe,” he added.

All-Kerala Chemists and Druggists Association (AKCDA) president A.N. Mohan said that the ability to procure medicines from outside Keralam has increased the risk of spurious and substandard medicines entering the market. He added that, as per their understanding, medicines allocated for Central government departments such as the Railways and Defence, which are provided at special rates, are obtained by middlemen from other States through clandestine methods.

“These are then sold and end up entering our markets when retailers purchase them from other States. It makes it difficult to trace where the medicines are arriving from. Some new-generation outlets that offer huge discounts have entered the picture, and their sole focus is on making profit,” said Mr. Mohan. He added that the only way to weed out the middlemen involved in the process was to bring in restrictions on procuring medicines from other States.
